jobs.brief: Hoa Lư, Đinh court, late tenth century Đại Cồ Việt. Archaeology documents reddish-brown fired-clay bricks and tiles, timber structures, stone column bases and lotus-decorated tile ends, rather than the old sprite's yellow thatch-like roof. Draw a dignified early royal precinct: a broad RED-BROWN TILED timber audience hall on a low stone/brick plinth, a smaller rear hall behind its roofline, two flanking low administrative/residential halls and a substantial single-storey tiled timber entrance pavilion, joined by low reddish brick enclosure sections with a slightly irregular plan. This is an illustrative grouping, no invented exact hall names or bay counts. Use warm terracotta roofs, ochre timber and a restrained vermilion accent on important columns, muted cream stone; broad low eaves with restrained tips, small lotus tile-end accents. Make a rich, dense roof ensemble within the old near-square footprint, width-to-height about 0.97. Do NOT copy the present seventeenth-century Đinh memorial temple, do NOT depict Early Lê gold/silver palaces as Đinh fact, no grand glazed golden roofs, pagoda towers, tall fortified gate towers, limestone scenery or Huế gate.

jobs.brief: Thăng Long, Lý dynasty, eleventh–twelfth century. The heritage centre describes a principal audience hall flanked by other halls, rear royal halls, and covered galleries surrounding the royal court. Reconstruct a compact precinct with a central audience hall, one visible smaller rear roof, two flanking halls and long roofed galleries, a front timber ceremonial entrance pavilion and low brick/earth-toned enclosure. Palace roofs may use GREEN and YELLOW glazed tiles; use graceful jade-green lateral roofs and an ochre-gold main roof, red/ochre timber, cream bases, small terracotta dragon/phoenix and bodhi-leaf ridge silhouettes. These are archaeological decorative forms, not immense roof monsters. Roof count and layout are illustrative, no claimed exact reconstruction. Poised upward eave tips, deep readable royal eaves, no tall pagoda. Footprint nearly square width-to-height 1.0. No later stone Đoan Môn gate, no Kính Thiên Lê staircase or Huế Ngọ Môn, no generic Chinese imperial gate.

jobs.brief: Đông Kinh / Thăng Long, Later Lê imperial palace precinct, centred on a cautious archaeological interpretation of Kính Thiên. Emphasise a broad ochre-gold glazed-tile ceremonial hall with a layered hipped roof over red timber columns, on a modest elevated pale-stone platform. The attested front staircase has THREE parallel approaches divided by FOUR stone dragon balustrades; make these small but visible. Behind and on both sides are lower palace roofs and covered galleries, creating a dense royal ensemble. Foreground: low, broad U-plan brick-and-stone Đoan Môn-inspired gateway with FIVE actual arched passages across its front. Do NOT copy the later Nguyễn upper pavilion as a securely known fifteenth-century design; a simple parapet on the gateway is sufficient. Outer enclosure quiet warm brick, the main hall gold/ochre and vermilion. Keep the hall to about 40% of compound width, not a towering palace filling everything. Exact timber superstructure is a reconstruction; do not reproduce nineteenth-century Long Thiên photographs as fifteenth-century fact. Overall compact near-square footprint width-to-height 0.99. No Hanoi Flag Tower (nineteenth century), no Huế gate, pagoda towers or modern flags.

jobs.brief: Huế imperial precinct under Minh Mạng after 1833, Nguyễn dynasty. The unmistakable foreground landmark must be the REAL TYPE of Ngọ Môn: broad low U-shaped BRICK/STONE PLATFORM, THREE arched passages in its front centre plus TWO passages in the projecting side returns (five total, NOT five identical front arches). Above it a graceful TWO-STOREY timber Ngũ Phụng pavilion running across the U with nine roof sections: central imperial roof GOLDEN YELLOW, surrounding wing roof sections GREEN glazed tile. Preserve the wide, horizontally articulated profile and projecting side wings; no single oversized central red roof. Behind the gate on the centreline show the wider low paired-roof Thái Hòa audience hall with golden-yellow tiles and vermilion columns, then one modest rear royal roof, with smaller green/red palace wings at either side. Narrow visible transparent court gap between gate and hall, no continuous ground tile. Muted ochre/cream masonry, red timber, gold and jade-green glazed roofs, restrained dragon ridge accents. Beautiful ceremonial sequence with 6–7 clear large roof groupings, width-to-height about 1.34 to keep the approved broad footprint. No Kiến Trung European-style twentieth-century palace, no European bastion invented onto the imperial gate, no Chinese Tiananmen/Forbidden City, no pagoda, flags or text.
